title: The same write delivered twice at the same time

R1.reason: idempotency_keys table with PK (tenant_id, user_id, operation, key), a fingerprint column, in PostgreSQL. The client reuses one key per tap on retry, and a retention purge is included.

R2.reason: The key claim, voucher update, ledger insert and stored response all run in one transaction. A concurrent duplicate blocks on the unique index and then replays. lock_timeout is mapped to 409 IN_PROGRESS with Retry-After.

R3.reason: The code compares the stored fingerprint with the new one and throws 409 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED on a mismatch. A test covers it.

R4.reason: UNIQUE (source_type, source_id) on credit_ledger, plus the conditional UPDATE on vouchers.redeemed_at IS NULL, give a business-level second guard.

R5.reason: Tests use real PostgreSQL with Promise.all concurrent requests, for same key and for different keys. The answer states they were not run.

forbidden.item: In-memory deduplication or a Redis TTL key as the only guard
forbidden.evidence: The answer rejects in-memory flags and Redis SETNX with a TTL, and uses PostgreSQL constraints.

forbidden.item: "Check then insert" without a unique constraint
forbidden.evidence: It uses INSERT ... ON CONFLICT on a primary key and an atomic conditional UPDATE. It explicitly rejects SELECT-then-INSERT.

forbidden.item: Relying on a queue job id for uniqueness
forbidden.evidence: No queue job id is used for uniqueness.

forbidden.item: Telling the client to generate a new key on retry
forbidden.evidence: The client is told to send the same key on every automatic retry. A new key is only for a new tap after a definite failure.

grade.summary: The answer fully meets all five rubric items, with the key table, fingerprint, single-transaction handling, a business unique constraint and concurrent PostgreSQL tests, and it violates no forbidden decision.
